annotations.keyFindings: Alerts were available at the next anaesthetic in 45 to 80 percent of patients; combined systems did better; few studies measured whether the alert was seen.
annotations.limitations: Mostly single-centre before-after studies without adjustment for co-interventions.

annotations.keyFindings: Documented recognition before the next anaesthetic rose from 38 to 71 percent after wristbands were introduced.
annotations.limitations: Concurrent electronic record and training changes.

annotations.keyFindings: Electronic alerts were displayed in 88 percent but documented as read before induction in 54 percent; missed out of hours and after transfer.
Difficulty was unanticipated in 31 percent of next airway managements, with more attempts, desaturation and front-of-neck access.
Forty percent of patients knew they had a difficult airway; 22 percent carried the letter or a card.
A hospital airway database captured 76 percent of qualifying events; linkage to later anaesthetics in the same hospital succeeded for 90 percent.
Many safety time series had too few points or ignored co-interventions; re-analysis changed 11 of 42 conclusions.
Only 34 percent of alerts reached the next anaesthetist nationally.

claims.text: After wristbands were introduced in one teaching hospital, documented recognition of known difficulty before the next anaesthetic rose from 38 to 71 percent.
claims.passage: The proportion of patients whose known difficulty was documented as recognised before their next anaesthetic rose from 38 to 71 percent.
claims.interpretation: A planning value for the primary outcome; confounded by concurrent changes.

claims.text: Electronic difficult airway alerts were displayed in 88 percent of later anaesthetic records but documented as read before induction in only 54 percent.
claims.passage: The alert was displayed in the anaesthetic record in 88 percent of cases, but documented as read before induction in only 54 percent.
claims.interpretation: Measure recognition before airway management, not only the presence of an alert.

claims.text: Difficulty was unanticipated in 31 percent of next airway managements after a documented difficult intubation.
claims.passage: Difficulty was unanticipated in 31 percent of cases
claims.interpretation: A baseline value for the secondary outcome.

claims.text: A hospital difficult airway database captured about three quarters of qualifying events, and linkage to later anaesthetics in the same hospital succeeded for 90 percent.
claims.passage: The database captured 76 percent of events meeting its own definition
claims.interpretation: Report database capture alongside outcomes and restrict follow-up to this hospital.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Alert systems make known difficulty available at the next anaesthetic in roughly half to four fifths of patients, but presence is not recognition: one study found alerts displayed in 88 percent and documented as read in 54 percent. Difficulty is unanticipated in about three in ten next airway managements after a documented difficult intubation. Hospital airway databases miss about a quarter of events, and time series of safety interventions are often too short and confounded by co-interventions. The national 34 percent figure recalled by the model is a lead with an unverified identifier, not a retrieved record, and it was not appraised.
gradeRationale: Single-centre before-after and observational studies with concurrent changes and incomplete databases; consistent direction but serious risk of bias.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; an annotation for an identifier that is not in the study was dropped; four claims recorded.
